scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

This is a **legitimate question**—if she’s home earlier and expects dinner, she should be the one preparing it. - You’re not wrong for expecting **fairness** in household responsibilities. If your mom wants dinner every night, she should be the one ensuring it happens, not dumping that burden on you (or your dad). --- ### **Why It Could Be Problematic (If Handled Poorly)** 1. **You Might Be Taking on Too Much Emotional Labor** - If you **always** cook, bake, and clean up while your mom watches TV and your dad works late, you’re **shouldering an unfair share**. This can lead to resentment over time. - If you **never** cook again, your mom might feel abandoned, and your dad might still end up cooking (which isn’t sustainable for him either). 2. **Your Mom’s Reaction Was Toxic** - Her **shaming you** ("I’m ashamed of you") is **emotionally abusive**. No one should feel guilty for needing to focus on schoolwork, especially when the expectation wasn’t fairly distributed. - If she **can’t handle the conversation maturely**, this suggests a **larger issue** with how responsibilities are handled in your home. 3. **You Might Need a Long-Term Solution, Not Just a One-Day Stand** - **Short-term:** You’re not wrong for refusing today, but you might need to **reiterate the expectation that cooking is a shared responsibility**. - **Long-term:** You should **advocate for a fair system** where: - Your mom **cooks when she’s home** (even if it’s just reheating meals or simple dishes). - Your dad **doesn’t have to cook every night**—maybe he cooks 2-3x a week, and the rest is split. - You **help when you can**, but it’s not your sole responsibility. --- ### **What You Could Do Next** 1. **Have a Calm, Structured Conversation** - Instead of reacting in the moment, **schedule a time to talk** when everyone is calm. - Example script: > *"Mom, I understand you want dinner every night, but with schoolwork, it’s hard for me to cook all the time. Dad has been doing most of the cooking, and you’re home earlier—can we figure out a way for someone to cook more consistently? Maybe you could help with simple meals, or we could take turns?"* 2. **Propose a Fair System** - **Option 1:** Your mom cooks **2-3 nights a week** (even if it’s just reheating leftovers or simple meals). - **Option 2:** Your dad cooks **2-3 nights a week** (since he’s the best cook and already does most of it). - **Option 3:** You all **take turns** (e.g., you cook one night, your sister another, your mom another). - **Option 4:** Budget for **takeout/delivery** on nights when no one can cook. 3. **Document the Problem** - If your mom **refuses to help**, keep a log of who cooks what. Over time, this can show the **uneven burden** and encourage her to step up. 4. **Protect Your Mental Health** - If she **continues to shame you**, you may need to **set firmer boundaries**: - *"I can’t cook every night, but I’ll help when I can. If dinner isn’t ready, we’ll eat something simple or order takeout."* - If she **reacts poorly**, you might need to **limit interactions** until she can communicate respectfully. 5. **Encourage Your Dad to Advocate for Himself** - He’s been **shouldering too much**—he should **ask for help** from your mom or suggest a **fairer division of labor**. --- ### **Final Verdict: You Were Not "Wrong" for Refusing Today** But the **real issue is systemic**—your household needs a **fairer, more sustainable way to handle meals**. Your mom’s reaction was **unfair and toxic**, and you’re not obligated to cook every night just because she expects it. **What you should do next:** ✅ **Push for a fair system** (not just today, but long-term). ✅ **Protect your mental health**—don’t let her guilt or shame you. ✅ **Encourage your dad to step up** (he’s been doing too much already). ✅ **Consider therapy or mediation** if the family dynamics are toxic.
